newsitem.title: UK: UK gilts recoup early gains after soft Philly Fed.
newsitem.headline: UK gilts recoup early gains after soft Philly Fed.

text.p: UK gilts ended the day in fine fettle, recouping morning gains late in the afternoon session after a weak U.S. Philly Fed survey report.
Softer-than-expected domestic inflation data helped the market up in the morning, although signs of cost pressures from the services industries and some goods sectors eroded some of the gains.

"The inflation data helped the market up a bit early on, but there are some concerns still about the pressures coming through from services," said a trader at a GEMM. "The main weakness in RPI has come from food prices and that could soon reverse."
UK underlying inflation grew 2.7 percent in the year to March compared with 2.9 percent in the year to February.
June gilt futures settled at 110-05, up 15/32.
The Philly Fed's business activity index fell to 5.7 in April from 21.1 in March, sparking a swift lurch upward in U.S. Treasuries.
"That allowed gilts to get back to earlier highs," the trader said.
Philip Shaw, group economist at Union Plc said U.S Treasuries were helping support European markets across the board.

"There is a feeling the downturn in U.S. bonds was overdone and that's helped sentiment everywhere." He said UK M4 data would be the main domestic event on Friday. The Reuters consensus forecast suggests M4 grew 11.0 percent in the year to March, slightly slower than February's 11.2 percent growth. "The market will keep half an eye on election developments, but there isn't much going on there to move gilts at the moment," said Shaw.
The yield spread between gilts and Bunds narrowed to 181 basis points from 183 on Wednesday.
Short sterling also benefited from the better inflation data. June settled at 93.46, up 0.03 while September settled at 93.20, also up 0.03.
"The strip is still factoring in a rate rise by the end of the second half, but really only a quarter point comfortably," said the trader.
"And if the data continues to come in softer June could still go a bit better, although with a change of Chancellor likely (after the May 1) election no-one wants to take too much of a punt on that."
